kit.title: Set up your group and run a session
kit.html:
By the end of this lesson you will have a date, a room, a list of men and a printed stack of worksheets, and you will know exactly what happens in each of the 75 minutes of a session. Every session in this guide uses the same shape, so once you've run one, you can run all seven.

You don't need to be a teacher, a counselor or the most disciplined man in the room. Your job is to keep time, ask the questions, and make sure every man leaves with one written commitment and a partner who will ask about it.

Who to invite

The kit works best with 4 to 12 men. Below four, one absence kills the room. Above twelve, men stop talking and start listening, and this material only works if they talk. If you have more than twelve, run two groups on different nights.

Invite men who keep making the same promise: to be more present, to pray with their wives, to put the phone down, to be patient with their children. You are not looking for men who have it together. You are looking for men who are tired of meaning it and changing nothing.

Ask personally. A bulletin announcement gets you three men. A conversation in the parking lot gets you the right ten. Say it plainly: "Seven weeks, one night a week, 75 minutes. We each leave with a plan that has a time on it. Will you come?"

What to print before night one

  • One copy of each of the seven step worksheets per man, from your download page
  • One Weekly Scorecard per man per week, or print a stack of 8 each
  • A sign-in sheet with each man's name, phone number and email
  • Two pens per man, because someone always forgets
  • A copy of the partner agreement in this lesson, one per pair

Your licence covers printing for every man in your group, for as long as your ministry runs it. Hand out each worksheet on the night it's used, not all at once, so nobody reads ahead and skips the work.

The shape of every session

Each session plan in the next module follows this 75-minute outline. The times matter. A session that runs long teaches the men that the plan is optional, which is the opposite of what this material teaches.

  1. Open, 5 minutes. Welcome, a short prayer, phones face down on the table.
  2. Report, 15 minutes. Each man says his number from the week: "I said Monday and Thursday at 7:40. I did it once out of two." Numbers only, no stories yet. From session 2 onward this is the most important part of the night.
  3. Teach, 15 minutes. You read or summarise the teaching in the session plan and read the named passage aloud.
  4. Talk, 15 minutes. Two or three of the discussion questions. You don't need all of them.
  5. Write, 15 minutes. Quiet time on the worksheet. Men write. You write too.
  6. Commit and pray, 10 minutes. Each man reads his one commitment for the week aloud to his partner. Partners pray for each other. Close.

Pair every man before he leaves night one

The accountability is what makes this different from a Bible study with homework. Pair men up on night one, two by two, with one group of three if your number is odd. Pair men who don't already talk every day; old friends go easy on each other.

Read this agreement aloud and have each pair say yes to it:

"Once a week, on the night we pick, I'll text you one word about my commitment: done, or missed. If I haven't texted by the next morning, you'll ask me. When I miss, you won't preach. You'll ask: what's the plan for next time?"

That's all. It takes thirty seconds a week, and it's the part men tell you about months later.

A worked example

Here is how a hypothetical first night goes for a leader with nine men in a fellowship hall on a weeknight at 6:30. He has the room set with one table, nine chairs and the Step 1 worksheets face down. He opens with prayer at 6:30 sharp even though two men are still parking. There's no report on night one, so he uses those 15 minutes to have each man answer one question: "What promise have you made more than twice?" He teaches from the session 1 plan, asks two questions, and gives 15 quiet minutes to the worksheet. At 7:35 he pairs the men, reads the partner agreement, and each man reads his sentence to his partner. They pray in pairs and he closes at 7:45. Two men stay to talk. He lets them, but the session itself ended on time.

Check yourself before night one

  • You have a fixed day, start time and end time for all seven weeks
  • At least four men have said yes to you personally
  • Worksheets for session 1 are printed, one per man
  • You've decided how you'll pair men if the number is odd
  • You've done the Step 1 worksheet yourself, so you know what you're asking

If all five are true, you're ready. Open the session 1 plan and run it as written the first time. You can adapt it once you've seen how your men respond.

About the licence: this kit is licensed to one church or ministry for its own men's groups. Print as many worksheets as your men need. Please don't resell it or share the download link outside your ministry.

kit.title: Session 1: decide who you are building
kit.html:
What every man leaves with: one written sentence describing the man he is becoming, read aloud to his partner.

Hand out: the Step 1 worksheet, "What type of man do you want to be?"

Read aloud: Ephesians 4:22 to 24.

Night one has no report, because nobody has a number yet. Use the first 15 minutes for introductions instead: each man gives his name and answers one question, "What promise have you made more than twice?" Go first, and be honest. The room will match the level you set.

The teaching, in your own words

Most men start with goals: lose twenty pounds, pray every morning, stop yelling. That's why the goals don't hold. A goal with no man behind it is a wish with a deadline. When the goal gets hard, there's nothing underneath it to hold it up.

So we start one step earlier. Before we decide what to do, we decide who is doing it. Paul tells us to put off the old self and put on the new one. That isn't a mood. It's a decision about identity, and it comes first.

Tonight each of you writes five attributes of the man you want to be, what each one looks like on an ordinary Tuesday, and how the people in your house would know it without you telling them. Then one sentence that holds all of it. That sentence becomes the standard every other step gets checked against.

Discussion questions (pick two or three)

  • Who is a man you've watched up close who was the same at home as he was in public?
  • Which of your promises was really about how you look, not who you are?
  • What would your children say you're like on a weeknight?
  • Where does Ephesians 4 say the change happens, and why does that order matter?

What a finished sentence looks like

Too vague: "I want to be a better husband and father." Nobody could tell whether that happened.

Usable: "I am a man who is home when he's home, keeps his word to his wife, and prays with his children before they sleep." Someone in his house could watch for each part of that.

During the writing time, walk the room. If a man's sentence could describe anyone, ask him: "How would your wife know?" Then let him rewrite it.

Commit and pray

Pair the men using the partner agreement from the setup lesson. Each man reads his sentence to his partner. The commitment for the week is simple: tape the sentence somewhere you'll see it every morning, and text your partner "done" when it's up.

Partners pray for each other by name. Close on time.

Leader check after the session

  • Every man has a sentence written in his own hand
  • Every man has a partner and the partner's number
  • You finished within five minutes of your end time
  • You know which men struggled to write, so you can call them this week

Session 2 starts with each man reading his sentence again, so it needs to be in his pocket next week.

kit.title: Session 2: cut to three goals
kit.html:
What every man leaves with: exactly three goals, each tied to a word in his sentence from session 1.

Hand out: the Step 2 worksheet, "What are your goals?"

Read aloud: Philippians 3:13 and 14.

Report (15 minutes)

Go around the table. Each man reads his sentence and says one thing: is it taped up, yes or no? Don't let anyone explain a no yet. You're teaching the room that a report is a fact, not a story. Thank each man and move on.

The teaching

Most men are carrying ten goals: the gym, the budget, the temper, the phone, the prayer life, the side business, the marriage, the kids' homework. Ten goals means none of them gets a time. Paul says "one thing I do." Not ten.

Tonight each man lists every goal he's carrying, then holds each one up against his sentence and asks: does this make me more like that man? He keeps three and crosses out the rest. Not forever, just for these seven weeks.

Here's the hard part to say out loud: if a goal doesn't answer to your sentence, it's somebody else's goal. Your father's, your pastor's, the man on your phone. Some good goals get crossed out tonight, and that's the point.

Discussion questions

  • Which goal have you started the most times?
  • Which of your goals did someone else hand you?
  • What did Paul have to leave behind to say "one thing I do"?
  • What will it cost you to cross out the goal you most want to keep?

Watch for this during the writing

Some men will keep three goals that are really one goal said three ways, like "pray more," "read my Bible" and "grow spiritually." That's fine if it's honest, but ask them to merge it into one and pick two more. Others will try to sneak in a fourth. Hold the line at three. The limit is the lesson.

A hypothetical example: a man starts with nine goals. His sentence says he "is home when he's home." He keeps "phone away during dinner and bedtime," "one date night a month" and "coach my son's practice twice a week," and crosses out the promotion, the half-marathon and the garage. He looks unhappy. Tell him that's what it looks like when a goal finally has room to work.

Commit and pray

Each man reads his three goals to his partner. The commitment for the week: tell one person at home which three you kept, and why. Text your partner "done" or "missed" once a week, on the night you agreed.

Partners pray over each other's three. Close on time.

Leader check

  • Every man has three goals, no more
  • Each goal connects to a word in his sentence
  • The report stayed under 15 minutes
  • Men who said "no" in the report got a call from you this week

Session 3 asks what has stopped these three goals before, so the list needs to come back next week.

kit.title: Session 3: name what has stopped you
kit.html:
What every man leaves with: one written sentence describing the exact moment his most important goal usually falls apart.

Hand out: the Step 3 worksheet, "What has stopped you so far?"

Read aloud: Romans 7:15 to 25.

This is the session where the room gets honest or doesn't. Your tone sets it. Go first in the report and first in the discussion, and name something real.

Report (15 minutes)

Each man says whether he told someone at home about his three goals: yes or no. Then one sentence on how they reacted. Keep it short. The stories can come out in the discussion.

The teaching

Paul describes doing the very thing he hates and not doing what he wants. Every man in the room knows that experience. The question tonight is not whether you've fallen short. It's where, exactly.

Most men didn't fail for lack of wanting it. Something stopped them, and it was usually the same thing every time. It's rarely a character flaw. It's a moment: a plan that depended on how you felt, one bad day that turned into a bad month, an evening with no decision in it, a habit you inherited and never agreed to.

Tonight each man takes his most important goal, thinks back to the last time it fell apart, and finishes this sentence: "It stopped when..."

Useful answers and useless ones

Useless: "I lack discipline." "I'm lazy." "I got distracted." You can't plan around any of those.

Useful: "It stopped when I got home after 7 and turned the TV on before I took my shoes off." "It stopped the first Sunday I missed, because I felt I'd already ruined it." "It stopped when my wife asked me about it and I got defensive." Each of those is a moment you could see coming.

When a man gives you a useless answer, ask him: "Where were you standing when it happened?" That usually gets you to the moment.

Discussion questions

  • What did Paul do with his frustration at the end of Romans 7?
  • Which habit did you inherit from your father that you never agreed to?
  • What time of day do your promises usually die?
  • What's the difference between shame about a miss and information from it?

Commit and pray

Each man reads his "It stopped when" sentence to his partner. The commitment for the week: notice the moment when it comes. Don't fix it yet. Just text your partner the day and time it happened.

Pray for each other specifically about that moment. Close on time.

Leader check

  • Every man wrote a moment, not a character trait
  • Nobody was pushed to share more than he chose to
  • You noted any man who mentioned something that needs a pastor or counselor, and followed up privately

If a man names abuse, addiction or an affair, this group is the wrong size of help. Talk with him privately this week and connect him to someone qualified.

Session 4 puts a time on the goal right where this moment sits, so the sentence needs to come back next week.

kit.title: Session 4: give each goal a time and a rule
kit.html:
What every man leaves with: his most important goal rewritten as a day, a time, a place and an action, plus a written line saying what counts as a miss.

Hand out: the Step 4 worksheet, "The laws of a system that holds," and the first Weekly Scorecard.

Read aloud: Luke 14:28 to 30, and Proverbs 21:5.

This is the session that changes things for most groups. Give the writing time its full 15 minutes even if the discussion is going well.

Report (15 minutes)

Each man says whether he caught his moment this week, and when: "Wednesday, 7:15, walking in the door." If he didn't catch it, that's a fine answer too. Write the times on a sheet as men say them. You'll use them in the teaching.

The teaching: four laws

Jesus says nobody builds a tower without sitting down first and counting the cost. A system is that counting, written down. Tonight we use four of its laws.

The clock law. Nothing exists until it has a time. "Weekly" is not a time. Thursday at 7:40 is. Across many studies, people who wrote down when and where they would act were measurably more likely to follow through than people who only decided to.

The source law. No source, no spend. Before your time, your money or your temper moves, name where it's coming from. The standard is scripture, not mood.

The failure law. Every system has a written way to fail. Decide what a miss looks like before you start, so one bad day doesn't cost you a month.

The evidence law. Numbers as numbers, not stories. Four out of seven is four out of seven, not "going well."

Worked example to read to the room

A man's goal is "phone away during dinner and bedtime." Last week he caught his moment: he walks in at 7:15 and checks his phone in the driveway before he comes inside.

His system: "Monday to Thursday, 7:15 PM, in the driveway, phone goes in the glove box until the kids are in bed."

His failure line: "A miss is any night the phone comes inside before 8:30. When I miss, I tell my wife that night and do it the next evening."

Notice that the time sits exactly where his wall was. That's the whole trick.

Discussion questions

  • Which tower have you started and left half-built?
  • Why does a written miss make it easier to keep going?
  • Where is your time going right now that nobody decided?

Commit and pray

Each man reads his system and failure line to his partner. Then he writes it on the Weekly Scorecard. The commitment: do it at the time you wrote, and fill in the Scorecard that night, every night, before next session. Text your partner your number once a week: something out of something.

Leader check

  • Every system has a day and a clock time
  • Every failure line describes something you could see
  • Every man has a Scorecard with his system written on it
  • Your own system is on your own Scorecard

From session 5 onward, the report is a number from the Scorecard. That's what makes the rest of the seven weeks work.

kit.title: Session 5: check the four pillars
kit.html:
What every man leaves with: his weakest pillar named, and one adjustment to his system based on last week's actual number.

Hand out: the Step 5 worksheet, "The four pillars," and a fresh Scorecard.

Read aloud: Joshua 24:15, and Ephesians 6:4.

Report (15 minutes)

This is the first real number. Each man reads his system and his count: "Four nights planned, two done." No explaining yet. Write every number down.

When the round is done, say what the numbers show without naming anyone: "Most of us kept about half. That's normal for week one of a system. Now we use it."

The teaching

Every part of a man's life lands in one of four places. Most men are strong in one and absent in another. Tonight each man checks all four.

Cycles: what you inherited and never agreed to. Systems: doing the right thing on a day you don't feel like it. Fatherhood: giving your children what you weren't given. Discipline: keeping going when nobody is watching.

Joshua decides for his whole house, out loud. Paul tells fathers not to provoke their children but to bring them up. Both are decisions made on purpose, not left to mood. The worksheet asks each man to rate himself in each pillar and pick the weakest one.

Use the number to adjust, not to judge

After the worksheet, each man looks at his own number and makes one change. Only one. The rules for a good change:

  • If he kept most days, keep the system the same for another week
  • If he missed at the same moment every time, move the time, not the goal
  • If he missed because the action was too big, make it smaller
  • If his weakest pillar isn't covered by any of his three goals, note it for session 7

A hypothetical example: a man planned prayer with his kids at 8:45 on four nights and did it once. Every miss was because the youngest was already asleep. He moves it to 8:00, right after baths. Same goal, new time. That's an adjustment. "I'll try harder" is not.

Discussion questions

  • Which pillar did your father leave you strongest in, and which weakest?
  • What would it sound like for you to say Joshua 24:15 in your own house?
  • What did your number tell you that you didn't want to hear?

Commit and pray

Each man tells his partner his weakest pillar and his one adjustment, and writes the adjusted system on his new Scorecard. Same commitment as last week: fill it in every night, text the number once a week.

Leader check

  • Every man reported a number, not a feeling
  • Every man made one adjustment, or chose on purpose to keep it the same
  • Nobody was shamed for a low number, including by himself

kit.title: Session 6: track it and report the number
kit.html:
What every man leaves with: systems for all three of his goals on one Scorecard, and an agreement with his partner to keep reporting numbers after the group ends.

Hand out: the Step 6 worksheet, "Why you need a system," and a fresh Scorecard.

Read aloud: Lamentations 3:40, and 2 Corinthians 13:5.

Report (15 minutes)

Numbers again, then one extra line from each man: "The adjustment I made last week did or didn't help." Compare this week's numbers with last week's out loud, as a group total. If the total went up, say so. If it didn't, say that too, and say it's information.

The teaching

"Let us search and try our ways." "Examine yourselves." Scripture assumes a man can look at his own life honestly and see what's there. The Scorecard is how you do that weekly instead of once a year at a conference.

You've been inspired before. A sermon, a conference, a video. It lasted until the middle of the week. Motivation is a feeling, and feelings have a shelf life. A system is what's still standing by Wednesday. It doesn't ask how you feel. It asks what time it is.

And tracking works best when someone else sees it. Across 138 experiments, people who monitored their progress reached more of their goals, and the effect was stronger when the progress was reported to someone else (Harkin and colleagues, 2016). That's why every man in this room has a partner.

During the writing time

Until now, most men have run a system for one goal. Tonight each man writes a day, time and failure line for his other two goals as well, all on one Scorecard. Three systems is the most a man should carry at once.

Walk the room and check each new system against session 4: does it have a clock time, and is the miss something you could see? Send back any that say "evenings" or "more often."

Discussion questions

  • What did you think when you first had to say your number out loud?
  • Who in your life already sees how you're doing, whether you tell them or not?
  • What will happen to your Scorecard the week after this group ends?

Commit and pray

Partners make one new agreement tonight: "After session 7, we keep texting our number every week for at least eight more weeks." Each man says it out loud. Then the usual commitment: Scorecard filled in nightly, number texted once a week.

Leader check

  • Every man has three systems on one Scorecard
  • Every pair has agreed to keep reporting after the group
  • You've decided what you'll offer the group after session 7 (see the final lesson)

kit.title: Session 7: put God at the center of the plan
kit.html:
What every man leaves with: his whole plan (sentence, three goals, systems, failure lines and numbers) on one page, prayed over and corrected, plus a plan for the next twelve weeks.

Hand out: the Step 7 worksheet, "God at the center."

Read aloud: Psalm 127:1, and Matthew 6:33.

Plan for this session to feel different. Slow the teaching down and give the prayer time more room than usual. You can take five minutes from the discussion to do it.

Report (15 minutes)

Each man gives his number for all three systems. Then the question that matters more than any number: "Has anyone in your house noticed anything, without you telling them?" Let men answer honestly, including "not yet."

The teaching

"Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain." Six weeks of building, and tonight we check whose house it is.

A system with you at the center will serve you. That's the problem. Built around yourself, even a good system becomes a more efficient way to get what you want. So the center isn't you. The man in your session 1 sentence starts as the man God is making. Your three goals answer to Him before they answer to you. The source law already said it: the standard is scripture, not mood.

"Seek first the kingdom." Not first the system, not first the number. The system is how a man keeps seeking on the days he doesn't feel like it.

The final writing time

Each man lays out everything from the seven weeks on one page: the sentence, the three goals, the three systems with their failure lines, and his numbers from sessions 5, 6 and 7. Then he prays over it silently and asks one question of every line: is this who God is making me, or who I want to look like? He changes anything that answers the wrong way.

A hypothetical example: a man realises his goal of "a second income stream by spring" was about looking successful to his brothers-in-law. He doesn't throw it out. He moves it below the two goals that are about his household, and gives it one evening a week instead of four.

Commit and pray

Each man reads his finished page to his partner. Partners confirm their eight-week reporting agreement from session 6. Then pray as a whole group, with each man praying one sentence for the man on his left.

Before you close, tell the group what happens next. The final lesson in this guide gives you three options.

Leader check

  • Every man has one page with his whole plan on it
  • Every partner pair has a reporting agreement for the next eight weeks
  • The group knows the date and shape of what comes next

kit.title: Keep the group going after week seven
kit.html:
Most men's groups end the same way: a good last night, a promise to keep in touch, and silence by February. The systems your men built only hold if someone keeps asking for the number. This lesson helps you choose what your group does next, and announce it on the night of session 7.

Option 1: a monthly report night

Meet once a month for 45 minutes. Each man reports his three numbers for the month, makes one adjustment, and prays with his partner. No new teaching. This is the lightest option and the one most groups can sustain all year.

Best for: groups where most men kept their numbers above half by session 7.

Option 2: run the seven sessions again

Start a new cycle with the same men, three months later. Each man writes a new sentence and keeps or replaces his goals. Men who've been through it once often go much deeper the second time, because they're no longer learning the method.

Best for: groups where several men struggled to get a system running, or where the group bonded and wants more time together.

Option 3: multiply

Ask two men from this group to lead the next one, with you sitting in for the first two sessions. Your licence covers every group your ministry runs, so there's no extra cost. This is how a men's ministry grows from one table to several.

Best for: groups with one or two men who clearly came alive during the seven weeks.

How to choose

  • Look at the group's numbers from session 7, not the mood of the last night
  • Ask the men privately which option they'd actually attend
  • Pick a date before session 7 so you can announce it that night
  • Whatever you choose, keep the partner pairs reporting every week

Your own check before you close the cycle

Before you plan the next thing, run the same test on your own life that you asked of your men: could someone in your house tell something changed in these seven weeks, without you telling them? A leader who keeps his own numbers is the strongest reason the next group will keep theirs.

If you or any of your men want to keep going individually, the Be The Man Club continues the same framework with new tools each month and a live monthly call. Couples in your group who want help together can ask about certified marriage counseling at bethemansystem.com.

ic.title: How the Inner Circle works
ic.html:
The Club gives you the system and a partner. The Inner Circle gives you me, ten men who know your name, and someone checking your number every week. This lesson is everything you need to use it. Read it once now and keep it bookmarked.

The weekly class

Thursdays, 7:00 to 8:00 PM Central, on Google Meet: meet.google.com/tcg-zspn-cco. Same link every week. The first class of the founding circle is Thursday, November 5.

The hour runs the same way every week. For ten minutes, each man gives his number from last week: kept days out of planned days. For twenty minutes I teach one thing. For the last thirty, two men take the hot seat: the group works through their system with them, out loud, until each leaves with one change and a time to do it. Everyone gets the hot seat about once a month.

Camera on, phone off the table. What's said in the room stays in the room. If you have to miss, text me before 5 PM that day.

Your monthly one-on-one

Forty-five minutes with me, once a month, on Meet or by phone. We go through your Scorecard for the month, your three systems, and whatever is in the way: at home, at work, in your walk. I'll email you within your first week to set the first one, and we book each next one before we hang up.

Your weekly Scorecard review

Every Sunday night, take a photo of your Weekly Scorecard and send it to me. By Tuesday you'll get one line back: what to keep, or what to change. Not a speech. One line you can act on.

A Scorecard with misses on it is exactly what I want to see. A blank one is the only kind I'll call you about.

Your direct line

Within 24 hours of joining, I'll text you from my number. Save it. Text or voice-note me on weekdays and I reply within 24 hours. Use it for the moment you're about to break a commitment, not just after.

This is a brotherhood of men, not counseling or crisis care. If you or someone in your house is in danger, call 911. If you're in crisis, call or text 988.

Everything else that's included

  • A half-day intensive every quarter, on Meet or in person in Huntsville, to build your next 90-day plan
  • Every live group I run, at no extra cost
  • One certified marriage counseling session for you and your wife each quarter
  • Everything in the Club: all seven steps, every tool, and the monthly Club call

Check yourself before your first class

  • The Thursday class is on your calendar, every week
  • You've saved my number when it arrives
  • You've printed this week's Scorecard
  • You've read the next lesson, Your first 30 days

ic.title: Your first 30 days
ic.html:
The first month decides whether the Inner Circle changes anything. Men who get value from a room like this do four things early: they finish Step 1, they pick three goals, they send a Scorecard every week, and they take the hot seat once. This lesson walks you through each one, week by week, so by day 30 you have a system running and a number to show for it.

Week 1: name the man

Open the members area and do Step 1, "What type of man do you want to be?" Twenty minutes, one sitting, a pen. Bring your one sentence to your first Thursday class and say it out loud. If it could describe any man, the room will tell you, and you'll rewrite it that night.

Week 2: cut to three

Do Step 2. Write every goal you're carrying, then keep three that answer to your sentence. Send me the three by text before Thursday. At your first one-on-one we'll check each one against what your house actually needs.

Week 3: give them times

Do Steps 3 and 4. Name the moment each goal usually dies, then give each goal a day, a time and a written miss. Here's a hypothetical example: "Phone in the glove box at 7:15 PM, Monday to Thursday. A miss is any night it comes inside before 8:30." Put all three on your Scorecard and send the first photo that Sunday.

Week 4: take the hot seat

Ask for the hot seat. Bring your first three Scorecards and one miss you want help with, in one line. The group will push on it. That's the point. You leave with one change and the time you'll make it.

How to know your first month worked

  • You have one sentence, three goals and three systems, all written
  • You sent a Scorecard photo four Sundays in a row, misses included
  • You took the hot seat once and made the change
  • Your number in week 4 is higher than in week 1, or you know exactly why not

If three of those four are true, the room is working for you. If they aren't, say so at your one-on-one. We'll fix the system, not your effort.
